title: Three acts can be the play
hookLine: the one who brought you on stage decides when you leave, and three acts can be a whole play (Meditations 12.36)
last: AN ENDING CAN ALSO BE A MEETING.

cards: There's a five-act plan a life is often expected to follow. School, then work, then love, then the house, then the long graceful ending. And a quiet worry comes with it: being behind.
Stuck in act two, as if the real story hasn't started yet. The last section of Marcus Aurelius's notebook, as we have it, answers with a surprising picture from the theater.

teach.b: Book twelve, section thirty-six, the end of the Meditations. An actor in a Roman theater is dismissed by the official who hired him for the show.

teach.h: BUT I'VE ONLY HAD THREE ACTS.
teach.b: The actor protests: but I haven't finished the five acts, only three.
Marcus answers, in George Long's 1862 translation: "Thou sayest well, but in life the three acts are the whole drama." What counts as a complete play isn't decided by the actor.
It's decided by whoever composed it in the first place. For Marcus, that's nature, the order of the whole, which brought you on stage and one day takes you off. Not a tyrant, not an unfair judge.
Then the book's last line, in Long's words: "Depart then satisfied, for he also who releases thee is satisfied." Marcus is not telling himself to hurry the ending.
He's telling himself to stop treating his life as a version. The fear of being stuck in act two assumes the play only counts once it reaches act five.

teach.h: NOT A Version: ALREADY A PLAY.
teach.b: Marcus turns that around: whatever acts you've had are already a real play, with its own shape and meaning.
You don't have to wait for a better ending to call it whole. Different traditions see what comes after death very differently, and elsewhere in the notebook Marcus weighs more than one possibility.
But on this point he's clear: the length isn't what makes it complete.

how: In modern Stoic practice, reflecting on mortality, called memento mori, is used to value the present rather than to dwell on death, and readers often turn to Meditations 12.36 for it.

o: the final act, where a Roman play reaches its end
a scene full of shouting, tears and conflict
a play, counted whole by its composer, not its length

games.q: the last section — tap the pairs.
p: decides when the play is whole

s: the Meditations ends with a picture from the theater
an actor dismissed after three acts: in life the three acts are the whole drama.
Marcus tells himself to hurry his ending
he tells himself to stop treating his life as a version; its length isn't what makes it whole.
Marcus was certain about what comes after death
elsewhere he weighs more than one possibility, and traditions see it very differently.

games.q: you're the actor. the official walks on stage after act three and says, that's all. what does Marcus say to you?
o: the three acts are the whole play; go satisfied.
games.why: Marcus says the one who composed the play decides when it's complete. "in life the three acts are the whole drama."

practice: Think of your life as a play in acts, and name each in a word or two: the first, the second, the one you're in now. Don't grade them; just notice there's already a shape here, people, turns, a few scenes that mattered.
Let it be a play, not a rehearsal, and if today feels heavy, let someone near you know.

wordCard.voice: Drama, the Greek word Marcus uses in Meditations 12.36: a play counted complete by its composer, not by its length. Today's word.
